planting.note: Sow fresh seed in fall so it experiences natural cold stratification over winter, since it forms a deep taproot in its first year and resents transplanting.

directions: Flat clusters of tiny yellow flowers open atop leafy stems in mid-spring, among the earliest umbellifer blooms available to newly emerged native bees and small native wasps. It is also a larval host for black swallowtail caterpillars, making it a quietly important spring link in the Texas Blackland and coastal prairie food web. Distinguished from the more northern Nuttall's prairie parsley by its restricted range through south-central and southeastern Texas into southern Oklahoma, it favors blackland clay, coastal prairie, and calcareous limestone soils. As a biennial-to-short-lived-perennial, it forms a basal rosette its first year and flowers the next, so let some seed heads mature and shatter to sustain the planting.

planting.note: Surface-sow onto well-drained, gravelly or calcareous soil, since seed needs light to germinate and rots quickly in heavy or waterlogged ground.

directions: Forms a low, hairy-leaved mound that stays in near-continuous bloom from spring through fall, covering itself in small white, aster-like ray flowers with yellow centers. Small native bees, flies, and beetles work the flowers for pollen and nectar, and it draws in skipper and other small butterflies as well. Native to the dry, rocky, calcareous uplands of West and Central Texas, Oklahoma, New Mexico, and northern Mexico, it thrives on neglect in gravelly or limestone soils and is a reliable, low-maintenance filler for xeriscape and rock-garden plantings. Its short-lived nature is offset by reliable self-seeding once established.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall as a winter annual; seed germinates with cooling temperatures and the rosette overwinters before blooming the following spring.

directions: True to its name, this evening primrose sends up no stem at all, instead holding large, fragrant, pale-yellow flowers flush against a ground-hugging rosette of lobed leaves. Each bloom opens in late afternoon and through the night, fading to pink by the next morning, timed to attract night-flying hawkmoths along with dusk-active bees. It is a winter annual (occasionally short-lived biennial) of blackland prairies, limestone glades, and playas from Missouri and Kansas south through Oklahoma, Arkansas, Louisiana, and Texas into northern Mexico. Its flat, stemless habit makes it an easy-to-overlook but rewarding choice for lean, dry, sunny soil at the front of a native bed.

planting.note: Direct sow after the soil has warmed into a consistently moist or wet, sunny site; it needs no stratification but will not tolerate dry ground.

directions: Slender, willowy stems carry small golden-yellow daisies from midsummer into late fall, later than most of its Coreopsis relatives, right as many other nectar sources are winding down. Bees and a range of butterflies work the flowers heavily during this late-season stretch. Native to wet pine savannas, sandhill seeps, wet prairies, and roadside ditches along the Gulf Coastal Plain from southeast Texas east to the Florida Panhandle, it wants consistently damp to seasonally wet, sunny soil and struggles in dry beds. Its narrow, grass-like leaves distinguish it from broader-leaved Coreopsis species, giving plantings an airy, see-through texture.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)

planting.note: Sow in fall into consistently moist to wet soil; cold-moist stratification over winter improves spring germination.

directions: Unlike its better-known relative Physostegia virginiana, this species blooms early, sending up spikes of pink to lavender tubular flowers from April into June along Gulf Coast prairies and marshes. Hummingbirds and long-tongued bees are the main visitors, with butterflies working the flowers as well, and like other false dragonheads each flower can be pushed sideways on its spike and will hold that position. Native to stream banks, swamps, floodplains, and shallow standing water across the Gulf Coast Prairies and Marshes, Texas Blackland Prairies, and adjacent Gulf Coastal Plain into Louisiana, it wants a consistently damp to wet site and does well at pond edges or in rain gardens. Its narrower, more open flower spikes and earlier bloom window set it apart from summer-blooming obedient plant.
